claims.text: Thermal-expansion mismatch is the primary cause of the unresolved stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Optimizing alloy composition can mitigate thermal-expansion mismatch.
Optimizing microstructure can mitigate thermal-expansion mismatch.
Reducing thermal-expansion mismatch reduces thermal stresses during composite solidification.
Reducing thermal stresses will improve stress–strain behavior.
Composition changes can alter the mechanical response of high-entropy alloys.
The relevant initial material is polycrystalline and may be a composite.
Controlled thermal-expansion measurements and simulation can isolate the proposed governing cause.
The proposed behavior is relevant under high-temperature conditions extending to 1250 °C.
The relevant temperature boundary is 293–1100 K.
Grain size may affect thermal expansion and stress–strain behavior.
Crystal structure may affect thermal expansion and stress–strain behavior.
An optimized composition should reduce thermal stress by at least 5% relative to the unoptimized baseline.
An optimized composition should improve stress–strain behavior by at least 10% relative to the unoptimized baseline.

contradictions.description: The conditions extend to 1250 °C (1523 K), whereas the stated response boundary ends at 1100 K, leaving the claimed upper-temperature regime outside the declared boundary.

The causal intervention is described as composition and microstructure optimization, but the intervention field specifies only measurement and simulation, which do not themselves create the proposed reduction in thermal-expansion mismatch.
